fixes.explanation: You got it, baker. The LORD tells Jeremiah, "Do not omit a word." (Jeremiah 26:2) Every word stays in. Skip the chocolate chips and that's not the recipe anymore. Jeremiah doesn't get to trim the message.

Right, the LORD doesn't say there's no chance. He says, "Perhaps they will listen and turn…" (Jeremiah 26:3) The aim is that they turn from their evil way of life, so that He may relent of the disaster He is planning. Perhaps is a small word, but it's holding a big door open.

That's the word, friend. The LORD says He will make the city "…an object of cursing among all the nations of the earth." (Jeremiah 26:6) That's a heavy line. It's the picture of what's at stake if they won't listen.

Envy would mean the nations wished they had the city. The LORD says the opposite: "…an object of cursing among all the nations of the earth." (Jeremiah 26:6) Cursing, not envy. It's a sobering picture.
The text doesn't show anybody grieving here. They seized him and shouted, "You must surely die!" (Jeremiah 26:8) I think that's anger aimed straight at Jeremiah. It's a hard moment.

That's what the crowd shouts. They say he dared to prophesy that "…this city will be desolate and deserted!" (Jeremiah 26:9) They say it right to his face. They repeat his message back at him, and I bet they are not happy about it.

Foreign kings never come up in the crowd's shout. They say he dared to prophesy that "…this city will be desolate and deserted!" (Jeremiah 26:9) A city under a foreign king still has people in it, baker. Desolate and deserted means nobody's home.

A split isn't what the crowd is yelling about here. Their words are, "…this city will be desolate and deserted!" (Jeremiah 26:9) I think they're upset that Jeremiah said it in the name of the LORD. Desolate and deserted is the answer.
Exactly. The priests and prophets tell the officials and the people that they know it "…as you have heard with your own ears!" (Jeremiah 26:11) That's their claim. No middleman, just ears.

The king isn't reading anything in this scene. The priests and prophets say, "…as you have heard with your own ears!" (Jeremiah 26:11) The officials did come up from the king's palace, but the priests and prophets point to hearing, not to the king.

No scribe shows up in this scene, friend. The priests and prophets say to the officials and people, "…as you have heard with your own ears!" (Jeremiah 26:11) That's what the priests and prophets are claiming: hearing, not reading. No paperwork involved, just ears.

Jeremiah never asks to be let go. He says, "…correct your ways and deeds, and obey the voice of the LORD your God…" (Jeremiah 26:13) Right after that he says, "…here I am in your hands…" (Jeremiah 26:14) He wants them to listen, not forget.

Yes, baker. Jeremiah says, "…you will bring innocent blood upon yourselves, upon this city, and upon its residents…" (Jeremiah 26:15) I think he's calm about it, even with a crowd around him. It's a serious warning.

Royal blood isn't what Jeremiah is talking about, friend. He says, "…you will bring innocent blood upon yourselves, upon this city, and upon its residents…" (Jeremiah 26:15) Innocent is the word he picks. And it lands in three places: on them, on the city, and on the people living in it.

That's it. The officials and all the people tell the priests and prophets, "This man is not worthy of death…" (Jeremiah 26:16) That's a big turn from the shouting earlier. And they say it straight to the priests and prophets.

Nobody mentions sending him out of the city. The officials and the people say, "This man is not worthy of death, for he has spoken to us in the name of the LORD our God!" (Jeremiah 26:16) That's the verdict and the reason together. Nothing about banishing him.

The king isn't part of their answer here, baker. They say, "This man is not worthy of death, for he has spoken to us in the name of the LORD our God!" (Jeremiah 26:16) That's what they tell the priests and prophets. Their reason is that he spoke to them in the name of the LORD their God.

Glory would be nicer to hear, baker. But the elders quote Micah as saying, "Zion will be plowed like a field…" (Jeremiah 26:18) Micah the Moreshite brought a hard message. That's the one the elders quote.

Not quite, friend. The elders ask, "Did Hezekiah king of Judah or anyone else in Judah put him to death?" (Jeremiah 26:19) Nothing in the text has Hezekiah putting Micah to death. Instead the elders say Hezekiah feared the LORD and sought His favor.

That's right, baker. The elders ask, "Did Hezekiah king of Judah or anyone else in Judah put him to death?" (Jeremiah 26:19) Nothing in the text has anyone putting Micah to death. The elders say Hezekiah feared the LORD and sought His favor.
That's right, baker. The text says, "…the king sought to put him to death." (Jeremiah 26:21) King Jehoiakim and his mighty men and officials heard Uriah's words. It's a heavy part of the story.
The text doesn't say anger. It says, "…he fled in fear and went to Egypt." (Jeremiah 26:21) Uriah found out the king sought to put him to death, and he fled. The word the text picks is fear.
